kit.name: ELEGOO UNO R3 Super Starter Kit

identity.manufacturer_part_number: none published by ELEGOO; functionally equivalent to Adafruit "Buzzer 5V - Breadboard friendly" (PID 1536)

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A tiny speaker that beeps on its own the instant you give it power, no special signal needed.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Sound alerts and alarms in a project; just set the connected pin HIGH or LOW.
function.how_it_works_briefly: It has a small oscillator circuit built in, so a plain steady voltage (not a changing signal) makes it vibrate at one fixed pitch and produce a tone.

pinout.notes: the longer of the two leads on a bare through-hole buzzer
the shorter of the two leads

pins.pin_1_identification: The positive lead is the longer of the two pins, the standard convention for this style of through-hole buzzer. ELEGOO's own diagram for the related passive buzzer wires the red jumper to positive and the black jumper to GND; the active buzzer follows the same colour convention.

electrical.operating_voltage: 3.5-5.5V DC (per the Handson Technology active buzzer module datasheet, a close equivalent element)
electrical.absolute_max_voltage: not published by ELEGOO; generic active buzzers of this type are typically rated up to about 5.5V
electrical.typical_current: about 30 mA at 5V DC (per the Handson Technology active buzzer module datasheet)
electrical.max_current: not published for this exact part; treat 30 mA as the expected draw at rated voltage
electrical.logic_level: 5V, works directly from an UNO digital output

key_specs.resonant_frequency_hz: approximately 2500 Hz +/- 300 Hz, fixed, cannot be changed by software

visual_identification.shape_and_size: Small round can about 12mm in diameter and roughly 9-12mm tall, with two pins sticking out of the bottom.
visual_identification.color_and_markings: The bottom is sealed with a solid black tape or sticker; this is how ELEGOO's own tutorial tells it apart from the passive buzzer, which shows a green circuit board instead.
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: Usually none visible once installed; may show a tiny voltage rating printed on the tape.
easily_confused_with: Passive buzzer (nearly identical size and shape, but has an exposed green PCB on the back instead of a solid black seal, and needs a changing signal rather than steady power to make sound)

example_connections.uno_pin: any spare digital output pin; ELEGOO's passive buzzer lesson uses D8, and the active buzzer lesson follows the same wiring style

wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: none required; driven with plain digitalWrite() HIGH/LOW

hazards: None significant; a low-voltage, low-current part
handling_notes: Observe polarity; reversed power usually will not damage it but will prevent it from sounding
common_mistakes: Confusing it with the passive buzzer and expecting tone() to change its pitch, it cannot, the tone is fixed

symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Leads reversed, or a passive buzzer installed by mistake
symptoms_and_causes.check: Look for a solid black sealed back (active) versus a green PCB (passive), and confirm the digital pin is being driven HIGH
Measure DC voltage at the buzzer's two pins with a multimeter while it is active; it should read close to 5V

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: Set the multimeter to DC voltage mode across the two pins while the UNO drives the connected pin HIGH; a working buzzer and correct wiring should read close to the supply voltage (about 5V). With power off, a working unit typically shows a stable low resistance through its internal coil in resistance mode.
